Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Manny Pacquiao's two-round demolition of Ricky Hatton has set up the prospect of the biggest money-spinning fight in the history of boxing. Pacquiao lands a solid right to Hatton on his way to a comprehensive victory. The Filipino knocked out the plucky but outclassed Briton in Las Vegas on Saturday night -- earning him by a conservative estimate at least $2 million dollars per minute. Hatton, who could well now hang up his gloves, will pocket more than $8 million as a consolation. Pacquiao's all-action style is popular with boxing followers and in his native Philippines the theaters which screened his fight live with Hatton were sold out well in advance with a ferocious demand for tickets. But the really big money lies in the Pay Per View (PPV) revenues generated by the U.S. Home Box Office (HBO) network. USA Today reported Monday that early indications from cable companies were that the scheduled 12-round light-welterweight bout could get as many as two million buys. Co-promoter Bob Arum was delighted with the figures especially as initial estimates were suggesting about one million boxing fans would shell out their cash. "We know based on those early numbers and based on experience the event will perform extremely well. If I had to guess, anywhere between 1.6 million and two million homes, which is a home run," he said. The record for a PPV event is the 2.4 million buys for 'Golden Boy' Oscar De La Hoya's May 2007 fight with Floyd Mayweather Jr., which generated a staggering $134 million in revenue. Mayweather, who also beat Hatton in another 'superfight' at the back end of 2007, astutely chose Saturday night in Vegas to announce he was coming out of retirement. Mayweather, nicknamed 'money' because of the enormous revenues he generates, will face Mexico's Juan Manuel Marquez on July 18 in his return to the ring. But the talk of the boxing world is an eventual match up against Pacquiao with the notional pound for pound title at stake as well as a massive pay day. "If Mayweather wants a piece of the 'little Filipino', just be my guest," Arum said before the dust had barely settled on the Hatton fight. With the flamboyant De La Hoya retired after being handed a painful beating by Pacquiao at the back end of 2008, the mantle of PPV king is set to fall to one of the two men who ended his ring career. Despite the global recession, the appetite for top prize fighting remains strong, but it is the more flamboyant characters who draw the biggest audiences. Last November's HBO clash between former pound for pound champion Roy Jones Jr. and the brilliant undefeated Welsh world champion Joe Calzaghe drew less than 250,000 buys. The only potential obstacle to a Pacquiao-Mayweather bout, the dangerous Marquez aside, is the relative sizes of the two men. Mayweather is a natural welterweight and would want a fight at 147 pounds, with Pacquiao, who started his remarkable career at light-flyweight, wanting the match at a lower weight. But big business and money is set to talk and many predict the showdown will come late this year, almost certainly in Las Vegas.

(CNN) — Manny Pacquiao’s devastating second-round knockout of Ricky Hatton has opened the door to what could become boxing’s most lucrative fight ever.

Pacquiao dominated the contest, landing a powerful right hand during his emphatic victory in Las Vegas on Saturday night. The Filipino fighter stopped the courageous but overmatched Briton and, even by cautious calculations, earned at least $2 million for every minute he spent in the ring. Hatton, who may now decide to retire, is expected to receive more than $8 million despite the defeat.

Pacquiao’s aggressive, action-packed approach has made him a favorite among boxing fans. In his home country of the Philippines, theaters showing the Hatton bout live sold out far in advance as demand for seats surged.

The greatest financial rewards, however, come from pay-per-view income through the U.S. network Home Box Office (HBO). USA Today reported on Monday that preliminary figures from cable providers suggested the planned 12-round light-welterweight fight might attract up to two million purchases.

Co-promoter Bob Arum welcomed the early results, particularly because original projections had estimated that roughly one million fans would pay to watch.

“Based on the initial figures and our previous experience, we know the event will do extremely well,” he said. “My estimate would be somewhere from 1.6 million to two million households, which would be a home run.”

The pay-per-view record remains the 2.4 million purchases generated by “Golden Boy” Oscar De La Hoya’s May 2007 bout against Floyd Mayweather Jr. That event produced an extraordinary $134 million in revenue.

Mayweather, who also defeated Hatton in another major fight late in 2007, strategically used Saturday night in Las Vegas to reveal that he was ending his retirement. Known as “Money” because of the huge sums his fights generate, Mayweather is scheduled to return against Mexico’s Juan Manuel Marquez on July 18.

Nevertheless, the matchup attracting the most discussion in boxing is a future contest between Mayweather and Pacquiao. Such a fight would offer an enormous payday while also determining the sport’s unofficial pound-for-pound supremacy.

“If Mayweather wants to take on the ‘little Filipino,’ he is more than welcome,” Arum said almost immediately after Pacquiao’s victory over Hatton.

De La Hoya retired after Pacquiao administered a punishing defeat to him late in 2008. As a result, boxing’s pay-per-view crown now appears likely to pass to one of the two fighters who brought De La Hoya’s career in the ring to an end.

Demand for elite prizefighting remains healthy despite the worldwide recession, although the sport’s most colorful personalities tend to attract the largest audiences. By comparison, HBO’s November fight between former pound-for-pound leader Roy Jones Jr. and unbeaten Welsh world champion Joe Calzaghe drew fewer than 250,000 pay-per-view purchases.

Apart from the threat posed by Marquez, the main possible barrier to a Pacquiao-Mayweather contest is the difference in their natural sizes. Mayweather is a genuine welterweight and would prefer to fight at 147 pounds. Pacquiao, whose remarkable career began at light-flyweight, would seek a lower limit.

The commercial stakes, however, are likely to prevail. Many observers expect the fight to happen near the end of the year, with Las Vegas considered the almost certain venue.

# Pacquiao flattens Hatton in second round, sets stage for Mayweather showdown

**LAS VEGAS —** Manny Pacquiao delivered one of the most emphatic victories of his career Saturday night, knocking out Ricky Hatton with a crushing left hook near the end of the second round at the MGM Grand Garden Arena.

Hatton fell heavily to the canvas with one second remaining in the round, prompting referee Kenny Bayless to stop the fight without a count. The British fighter remained on his back for several minutes before leaving the ring under his own power.

Pacquiao had already dropped Hatton twice in the opening round, repeatedly beating him to the punch with sharp combinations and superior speed. The victory gave the Filipino star Hatton’s junior welterweight title and strengthened his claim as boxing’s leading pound-for-pound fighter.

“I didn’t expect a short fight,” Pacquiao said afterward. “I was lucky to hit him with a right hook. That was the key.”

The result was a bitter disappointment for Hatton and the thousands of British supporters who traveled to Las Vegas. Hatton entered the bout with only one previous defeat, a 2007 stoppage loss to Floyd Mayweather Jr.

Attention now turns to a possible fight between Pacquiao and Mayweather — a matchup that could become one of the richest in boxing history.

Mayweather, unbeaten and a former champion in five weight classes, recently announced his return from retirement. His combination of defensive skill, speed and drawing power would make a bout with Pacquiao a major global event.

But several obstacles remain, including purse negotiations, weight and the fighters’ promotional interests. Mayweather has long considered himself boxing’s top attraction, while Pacquiao’s victories over Oscar De La Hoya and Hatton have dramatically increased his commercial leverage.

Pacquiao’s promoter, Bob Arum, said any future opponent would have to recognize the Filipino champion’s growing stature.

For now, however, Pacquiao has made the strongest possible statement. Two rounds were enough to dismantle Hatton — and to intensify calls for a showdown with Mayweather.

Pacquiao had taken Hatton’s junior-welterweight title while strengthening his claim as the sport’s pound-for-pound leader—a status Mayweather had held before retiring. Their contrasting styles, unbeaten-or-elite reputations, and huge pay-per-view appeal promised an enormous event.

# Boxing Business Analysis — May 2009  
## Pacquiao, Mayweather and the Fight That Could Break Every Revenue Record

Manny Pacquiao’s second-round destruction of Ricky Hatton on May 2 has changed boxing’s commercial landscape. Pacquiao is no longer merely an elite fighter with a passionate Asian following; he is becoming a global attraction capable of carrying major American pay-per-view events.

At the same time, Floyd Mayweather Jr. has announced his return from retirement to face Juan Manuel Márquez on July 18. That comeback appears designed to re-establish Mayweather’s position as boxing’s leading pay-per-view star—and to prepare the market for the one contest with substantially more earning potential than either man’s other options: Pacquiao versus Mayweather.

## Pacquiao’s rapidly expanding value

Pacquiao’s popularity rests on an unusually broad commercial base:

- **The Philippines:** He is a national institution, creating exceptional television audiences, sponsorship opportunities and political-level public interest.
- **The United States:** Victories over Oscar De La Hoya and Hatton have moved him beyond boxing’s core audience. Both bouts were marketed as mainstream sporting events.
- **Asian and international markets:** Pacquiao offers boxing a commercial bridge into territories that American promoters have historically struggled to monetize.
- **Hispanic fight fans:** His aggressive style and record against Mexican stars—including Marco Antonio Barrera, Erik Morales and Márquez—have given him significant recognition within one of boxing’s most important consumer groups.
- **Casual viewers:** Pacquiao’s speed, offense and knockout power make his fights easy to sell. Unlike many technically excellent champions, he rarely requires a complicated promotional explanation.

His December 2008 stoppage of De La Hoya reportedly generated roughly 1.25 million domestic pay-per-view purchases. The Hatton figures are not yet final, but the event benefited from strong American interest and a large British audience. The spectacular knockout should also improve Pacquiao’s future value: highlight-reel finishes are among the most effective advertisements for a boxer’s next event.

Pacquiao can now credibly claim to be boxing’s leading active attraction. The remaining question is whether he can match Mayweather’s proven record at the very top of the pay-per-view market.

## Why Mayweather is returning

Mayweather retired in 2008 while still undefeated and near the peak of his earning power. His return is unlikely to be motivated by competition alone. The sport has continued generating major purses, while Pacquiao has occupied the position Mayweather vacated as boxing’s unofficial pound-for-pound leader.

The Márquez fight serves several business purposes:

1. **It restores Mayweather’s visibility.** A retirement of less than two years is long enough to create demand but short enough to preserve his athletic relevance.
2. **It provides a comparison with Pacquiao.** Márquez fought Pacquiao twice in close, disputed contests. If Mayweather defeats him convincingly, promoters can use the result to strengthen the case for a Pacquiao showdown.
3. **It tests Mayweather’s current drawing power.** Pay-per-view sales will show whether his audience remained intact during retirement.
4. **It creates negotiating leverage.** Mayweather can argue for the larger share of a Pacquiao purse if his comeback performs strongly.

Mayweather remains a highly effective commercial personality because he is both admired and disliked. His undefeated record, defensive brilliance, public displays of wealth and confrontational promotional style give audiences a reason either to support him or pay to see him lose.

## Why Pacquiao–Mayweather could become boxing’s richest fight

The current commercial benchmark is Mayweather’s 2007 bout with De La Hoya, which generated approximately 2.4 million domestic pay-per-view purchases and more than $120 million in pay-per-view revenue. It also produced a record live gate of about $18.4 million.

Pacquiao–Mayweather could challenge or exceed those figures because it would combine several distinct markets rather than relying on one star’s audience.

### 1. Two genuine pay-per-view headliners

Most major boxing events feature one established attraction and an opponent. This would be different. Mayweather has already participated in boxing’s biggest pay-per-view event, while Pacquiao has now demonstrated that he can headline million-buy-level shows.

Their audiences are also complementary:

- Mayweather brings the American pay-per-view base, an undefeated record and the promotional “villain” role.
- Pacquiao brings Filipino, Asian and international interest, as well as fans attracted by action and knockouts.
- Both have strong recognition among Hispanic boxing consumers.
- Their shared connection to De La Hoya and Hatton gives casual fans an easy basis for comparison.

### 2. A simple, compelling narrative

The event would sell itself as a contest between:

- the two leading pound-for-pound fighters;
- Mayweather’s defense against Pacquiao’s offense;
- an undefeated former champion against boxing’s most explosive active star;
- the sport’s previous No. 1 fighter against the man who replaced him during retirement.

That clarity matters. The biggest events usually have narratives that can be understood by people who do not follow boxing every week.

### 3. Scarcity and uncertainty

There is no guarantee the bout will happen. Promotional rivalries, purse demands and disagreements over weight could prevent it. That uncertainty may increase demand if an agreement is finally reached. Consumers would view the contest as a rare event rather than another championship defense.

It would also be difficult to identify a clear favorite. Mayweather would have advantages in size, reach and defensive skill, while Pacquiao would bring speed, southpaw angles, activity and momentum. Competitive uncertainty supports stronger pay-per-view sales than a fight widely viewed as a mismatch.

### 4. Premium pricing opportunities

A Pacquiao–Mayweather promotion could maximize revenue through:

- a higher pay-per-view price;
- premium casino site fees;
- record-level ticket pricing;
- closed-circuit and theater distribution;
- sponsorships;
- international television rights;
- replay, home-video and digital rights;
- separate commercial arrangements in the Philippines and Britain.

Las Vegas would be the natural host because of its casino economics, although the scale of demand could revive discussion of a larger stadium venue. A casino might still offer more guaranteed money because it values high-spending visitors beyond the ticket revenue itself.

## Illustrative revenue potential

If the fight approached or exceeded the De La Hoya–Mayweather audience, its economics could look roughly as follows:

| Revenue source | Illustrative potential |
|---|---:|
| U.S. pay-per-view | $120 million or more |
| Live gate and site fee | $20–30 million |
| International rights | $10–25 million |
| Sponsorship, closed circuit and ancillary sales | $10–20 million |
| **Potential gross event revenue** | **$160–195 million or more** |

These are directional estimates, not forecasts. Distributor fees, promoter expenses, fighter guarantees and revenue-sharing arrangements would substantially reduce the amount available as profit. Nevertheless, the two fighters could plausibly divide purses larger than any previously paid for a single boxing match.

## The principal obstacle: dividing the money

The same commercial strength that makes the fight valuable could make it difficult to negotiate.

Mayweather can point to the De La Hoya and Hatton events and argue that he is the proven pay-per-view leader. Pacquiao can respond that he has become the sport’s most active global star, defeated both common opponents more decisively and is bringing momentum Mayweather currently lacks.

A straight 50–50 split may be the simplest solution, but neither side may initially accept it. Alternatives could include:

- a guaranteed purse plus a percentage of pay-per-view revenue;
- performance escalators based on purchase levels;
- a 50–50 division with separate treatment of Philippine or international rights;
- a rematch clause with the winner receiving the larger share of a second fight.

Promotional control is another issue. Pacquiao is represented by Top Rank, while Mayweather has worked closely with adviser Al Haymon and Golden Boy Promotions. Agreement would be required on lead promotion, television production, accounting, sponsorships and revenue reporting.

## Outlook as of May 2009

The business case is unusually strong, but the timing depends on both fighters continuing to win. Mayweather must first defeat Márquez and demonstrate that his comeback can still command a large audience. Pacquiao must decide whether to wait for Mayweather or pursue another lucrative bout, possibly at junior welterweight or welterweight.

If both remain victorious, Pacquiao–Mayweather would possess every ingredient required for a record event: elite sporting credibility, contrasting personalities and styles, global appeal, proven pay-per-view performance and genuine uncertainty about the outcome.

De La Hoya–Mayweather established how large a boxing event can become when a mainstream attraction meets an undefeated star. Pacquiao–Mayweather could go further by matching two fighters who each believe he is the sport’s true No. 1. In commercial terms, that disagreement may be boxing’s most valuable asset.

# Pacquiao win raises prospect of Mayweather megafight

**LAS VEGAS —** Manny Pacquiao’s stunning demolition of Oscar De La Hoya has reshaped boxing’s commercial landscape and intensified calls for a showdown with unbeaten former pound-for-pound king Floyd Mayweather Jr.

Pacquiao, moving up two weight divisions for Saturday’s welterweight bout, overwhelmed the taller and heavier De La Hoya with speed, movement and rapid combinations. De La Hoya remained on his stool after the eighth round, giving Pacquiao the most lucrative and high-profile victory of his career.

Promoter Bob Arum, who represents Pacquiao and once promoted Mayweather, said the result created an obvious next step if Mayweather could be persuaded to end his retirement.

“If Floyd Mayweather wants to come out of retirement, that’s the fight,” Arum said. “It’s the fight the public wants to see.”

Arum went further in assessing Pacquiao’s chances against the defensive master.

“The one guy who can beat Mayweather is Manny Pacquiao,” he said, arguing that the Filipino’s hand speed, unconventional angles and relentless work rate would present problems Mayweather has not faced before.

Mayweather retired in 2008 with a 39-0 record after victories over De La Hoya and Ricky Hatton. His split-decision win over De La Hoya in May 2007 set a pay-per-view record, attracting about **2.4 million domestic purchases** and generating roughly **$120 million in U.S. pay-per-view revenue**.

Those figures established Mayweather as one of the sport’s biggest attractions, while Pacquiao’s victory over De La Hoya demonstrated that he, too, could carry a major promotion.

The Pacquiao-De La Hoya event drew approximately **1.25 million U.S. pay-per-view buys**, producing about **$70 million in domestic pay-per-view revenue**. The total was especially impressive given the weakening economy and confirmed Pacquiao’s transition from international star to mainstream American attraction.

Arum said a Pacquiao-Mayweather contest could rival boxing’s largest events.

“It would be one of the biggest fights in the history of the sport,” he said. “You have two great fighters, two completely different styles and a fight that everybody would want to see.”

## De La Hoya’s future in doubt

For De La Hoya, the defeat appeared to mark the end of an era.

The 35-year-old American, a 1992 Olympic gold medalist and world champion in six weight divisions, had been boxing’s leading pay-per-view attraction for more than a decade. Nicknamed “The Golden Boy,” he combined crossover celebrity with a résumé that included bouts against Julio César Chávez, Pernell Whitaker, Félix Trinidad, Shane Mosley, Bernard Hopkins and Mayweather.

Against Pacquiao, however, De La Hoya looked slow and unable to cope with his opponent’s pace. His left eye swelled, his face absorbed repeated straight left hands, and he rarely mounted an effective attack. After consulting with his corner and the ringside physician, he declined to answer the bell for the ninth round.

“I have to see if I still have it,” De La Hoya said afterward, stopping short of immediately announcing his retirement.

His loss followed another sobering result for one of boxing’s best-known veterans. A month earlier, unbeaten Welshman Joe Calzaghe had dominated Roy Jones Jr. over 12 rounds at Madison Square Garden.

Calzaghe, a longtime super-middleweight champion, had moved to light-heavyweight and defeated both Hopkins and Jones during 2008. His victory over Jones took his record to 46-0 and strengthened his claim as one of the outstanding fighters of his generation.

Jones, by contrast, was a shadow of the athlete who had won titles from middleweight through heavyweight. Once celebrated for his reflexes, speed and improvisational brilliance, the former four-division champion had already suffered damaging knockout losses to Antonio Tarver and Glen Johnson. The defeat by Calzaghe further underlined the changing of the guard.

Pacquiao’s victory over De La Hoya carried the same message. The Filipino began his career at 106 pounds and won his first world title at flyweight. He later captured championships at junior featherweight, featherweight, junior lightweight and lightweight before jumping to the 147-pound limit to meet De La Hoya.

Trainer Freddie Roach, who had previously worked with De La Hoya, predicted before the fight that age and accumulated punishment had diminished the Golden Boy. Pacquiao’s performance proved that assessment emphatically correct.

## Marquez remains a rival

A Mayweather fight is not Pacquiao’s only option.

Mexico’s Juan Manuel Marquez continues to press for a third bout after two closely contested meetings with Pacquiao. Their first encounter, in 2004, ended in a draw despite Marquez being knocked down three times in the opening round. Pacquiao won the March 2008 rematch by split decision after scoring another knockdown, but Marquez and many of his supporters argued that the Mexican had done enough to win.

That second fight generated roughly **400,000 pay-per-view purchases**, a strong figure for the lighter weight divisions and evidence of the rivalry’s appeal.

Marquez subsequently stopped Joel Casamayor to win the lineal lightweight championship, establishing himself as a leading candidate for another meeting with Pacquiao. A third fight would settle unfinished business, though it would be unlikely to match the financial scale of a Mayweather contest.

Pacquiao also could return to junior welterweight or lightweight, with leading names in those divisions offering additional possibilities. But after beating De La Hoya, the focus has shifted toward the sport’s former No. 1 fighter.

## Obstacles to a deal

Negotiating a Mayweather-Pacquiao fight would not be straightforward.

Mayweather has given no firm indication that he intends to return, and disputes over the purse, promotional control and weight would be inevitable. He has also had a contentious relationship with Arum since leaving the promoter’s Top Rank organization.

Pacquiao, meanwhile, has emerged from the De La Hoya fight with enhanced bargaining power. Before the bout, some critics dismissed him as too small for a natural welterweight. After eight one-sided rounds, he was being discussed as boxing’s leading pound-for-pound fighter and one of its most marketable stars.

The contrasting styles would provide the central attraction: Pacquiao’s aggressive southpaw attacks against Mayweather’s precise counterpunching and defense. It would also match the sport’s reigning star against the unbeaten champion who walked away while still considered the best fighter in the world.

Whether Mayweather can be lured back remains uncertain. What is clear is that Pacquiao’s victory has given boxing a new dream fight — and enough pay-per-view evidence to make it a financial reality.
